rule: laten zien = normal spoken 'show'; tonen = formal, display, or demonstrate.

examples.nl: Kun je me dat laten zien?
Ik laat je mijn kamer zien.
examples.en: I will show you my room.
The screen shows an error message.

tips: laten zien literally means 'let see' — safest in all normal conversation.
tonen is common with screens, graphs, exhibits, signs, evidence, and emotions.
Perfect tense: Ik heb het hem laten zien. Do not say: Ik heb het hem gelaten gezien.
In class, 'Kunt u dat nog een keer laten zien?' sounds more natural than tonen.
teacherQuestion: When would tonen sound too formal in daily speech?

rule: wakker zijn = be awake; wakker worden = wake up; wakker maken = wake someone else; opstaan = get out of bed.

examples.nl: Ik word om zeven uur wakker.
Maak me om acht uur wakker.
Ik sta om half acht op.
examples.en: I get up at half past seven.
examples.note: Leave the bed / start the day.

examples.nl: Ik word om zeven uur wakker, maar ik sta pas om acht uur op.
examples.en: I wake up at seven, but I only get up at eight.
examples.note: Awake and out of bed are different.

tips: wakker zijn = to be awake (state).
wakker worden = to wake up / become awake (change).
wakker maken = to wake someone else up (cause).
opstaan = to get up, usually from bed.
teacherQuestion: Can opstaan also mean 'stand up' outside the bedroom context?

rule: Ik werd moe wakker = clean simple past. Ik ben moe wakker geworden = result still relevant now.

examples.en: This morning I woke up tired.
I woke up with a headache.

examples.nl: Ik ben vandaag moe wakker geworden.
Ik was moe toen ik wakker werd.
examples.en: I was tired when I woke up.

tips: Ik werd moe wakker is very natural when telling a past event.
Ik ben moe wakker geworden can feel like 'I have woken up tired today,' especially when the tiredness still matters now.
teacherQuestion: In spoken Dutch, which one would you personally say first?

rule: hersenen = biological brain; brein = brain / mind / mastermind; hersens = informal brains.

examples.nl: Zij is het brein achter het plan.
examples.en: She is the mastermind behind the plan.

tips: de hersenen is grammatically plural in Dutch when referring to the organ.
het brein can mean the organ, the mind, or the person behind a plan.
hersens is useful to recognise, but avoid it in formal writing.
teacherQuestion: When would you choose brein instead of hersenen in normal conversation?

rule: vroeg = early; eerder = earlier / sooner / previously; vroeger = formerly / in the past.

examples.en: Can you come a bit earlier?

examples.nl: Eerder vandaag heb ik hem gezien.

examples.en: I used to live in England.
Tomorrow I have to get up earlier.

tips: Do not translate every English 'earlier' as vroeger.
Use eerder when you mean before another time or sooner.
Use vroeger when you mean 'back in the past' or at an earlier clock time.
teacherQuestion: Are there situations where both eerder and vroeger are possible but the feeling changes?

rule: eerder compares moments in sequence; vroeger points to the past as a period or to an earlier clock time.

examples.en: In the past, I was often tired.

tips: eerder vandaag is normal; vroeger vandaag is usually unnatural.
eerdere versie = previous version.
vroegere leraar = former teacher.
teacherQuestion: Could you give me three natural sentences with eerder and three with vroeger?

rule: blijf (present) has a moving ij/ei diphthong; bleef (past) has a longer, steadier ee vowel.
tips: Practice in pairs: blijf/bleef, schrijf/schreef, rij/reed.
The ij sound is the same as ei — a moving diphthong.
The spelling difference alone is not enough — listen and copy the vowel shape.
teacherQuestion: Can you model blijf, bleef, schrijf, schreef slowly so I can copy the vowel movement?

topic: verlaten vs kwijtraken vs kwijt zijn
rule: verlaten = leave / abandon deliberately; kwijtraken = lose accidentally; kwijt zijn = be unable to find something right now.

examples.note: Grammatically correct but sounds formal. More natural in speech: Ik ga het gebouw uit / Ik ga weg uit het gebouw.
Sounds like abandonment — heavy. For ending a relationship, hij heeft het uitgemaakt is more natural.

examples.en: He ended the relationship. / He broke it off.
examples.note: Natural way to say someone ended a relationship.

examples.nl: Ik raak altijd mijn sleutels kwijt.
Ik heb mijn tas thuis laten liggen.
examples.en: I left my bag at home.
examples.note: Not verlaten — you left it behind. laten liggen = left it lying there.

examples.nl: Waar heb ik mijn sleutels gelaten?
examples.en: Where did I leave my keys?
examples.note: laten works naturally for misplaced objects: keys, phone, book, etc.

tips: verlaten sounds formal for leaving a building — prefer Ik ga het gebouw uit in everyday speech.
For ending a relationship, hij heeft het uitgemaakt is more natural than verlaten.
Do not use verlaten for accidentally losing a phone or keys.
Waar heb ik X gelaten? is natural for misplaced objects (sleutels, telefoon, boek).
kwijt zijn = current state: I cannot find it.
kwijtraken = the event: I lost it.
verliezen also means 'to lose', especially in games or competitions.
teacherQuestion: When would you use verliezen instead of kwijtraken?

rule: lenen van = borrow from someone; uitlenen aan = lend to someone.

examples.nl: Mag ik een pen van je lenen?
examples.en: Can I borrow a pen from you?

examples.nl: Ik leen een boek van Sam.
examples.en: I borrow a book from Sam.

examples.note: Owner gives temporarily — fine without uit for small everyday items.

examples.nl: Ik leen mijn fiets aan Lisa uit.
examples.en: I lend my bike to Lisa.
examples.note: uitlenen fits larger or special objects well.

examples.en: I lend my bike to Lisa.
examples.note: Also natural — without aan or uit.

examples.nl: Ik heb geld van mijn broer geleend.
examples.en: I borrowed money from my brother.

tips: When you are the borrower, say lenen van.
uitlenen fits larger or special objects — saying ik leen mijn pen uit sounds odd for small items.
geld uitlenen is also unusual, since you never return the exact same notes.
When you are the lender, Ik leen Lisa mijn fiets or Ik leen mijn fiets aan Lisa are both natural.
Mag ik even je pen lenen? is a very natural request.
teacherQuestion: In daily speech, do people prefer lenen or uitlenen when they mean 'lend'?

rule: Mag ik...? = normal and direct; Zou ik mogen...? = leaves more room for the other person to say no (not necessarily more formal — also used with friends); Is het goed als...? = asks if the situation is acceptable.

examples.en: May I go to the toilet?
Would it be OK if I sat here?
examples.note: Leaves space for the other person to say no — also natural with friends, not only in formal situations.

examples.nl: Zou ik vandaag iets eerder weg mogen?
examples.en: Could I leave a bit earlier today?

examples.nl: Is het goed als ik morgen later kom?
examples.en: Is it okay if I come later tomorrow?
examples.note: Checks if the situation is acceptable.

examples.nl: Is het goed als ik dit thuis afmaak?
examples.en: Is it okay if I finish this at home?
examples.note: als sends the verb to the end.

tips: Mag ik...? is not rude — it is normal.
Zou ik mogen...? is not necessarily more formal — Tessa uses it with friends too. It simply leaves more room for the other person to decline.
After als, put the verb at the end: Is het goed als ik eerder wegga?
teacherQuestion: Which form sounds most natural when speaking to you as my teacher?

rule: even often means 'just', 'briefly', or 'for a moment'. It softens requests and makes actions sound smaller.

examples.nl: Mag ik even je pen lenen?
examples.en: Can I just borrow your pen for a moment?
I will just have a quick look.
Can you help me for a moment?
I will give you a quick call.

examples.note: Friendly or direct, depending on tone.

tips: even can make a request sound smaller and easier to grant.
If the task is actually big, even can sound like you are minimising the effort.
Informal speech often uses effe — use even in class and writing.
teacherQuestion: When can even sound too casual or slightly pushy?

rule: Dutch mostly uses nog weten / niet meer weten instead of herinneren. nog weten = still remember (a fact); herinneren = recall an event or experience; onthouden = store in memory for later.

examples.note: Most natural everyday form. Literally: do you still know that?

examples.nl: Weet je nog dat we samen in Parijs waren?
examples.en: Do you remember that we were in Paris together?
examples.note: Weet je nog dat... = Do you remember that (something happened)?
Most natural spoken form for 'I still remember'.
Fact or piece of information still in memory.

examples.en: Now I remember! / I've just remembered!
examples.note: Use this when it suddenly comes back to you.

examples.nl: Het schiet me ineens te binnen.
examples.en: It suddenly comes to me. / I've just remembered.
examples.note: te binnen schieten = to suddenly come to mind.

examples.nl: Ik herinner me die dag nog goed.
examples.en: I still remember that day well.
examples.note: herinneren is natural for events and experiences — not for simple facts.

examples.nl: Ik kan me zijn naam niet herinneren.
examples.note: Trying to recall right now — natural with names, events, details.

examples.en: I have to remember this password.
examples.note: onthouden = store in memory for future use.

examples.nl: Denk eraan om melk te kopen.
examples.note: Remember to do something = Denk eraan... or Vergeet niet...

tips: nog weten is the everyday Dutch pattern — use it for almost everything.
'Do you remember X?' → Weet je X nog? or Weet je nog dat...?
'I still remember' → Ik weet het nog / Dat weet ik nog.
'I've just remembered!' → Nu weet ik het weer! or Het schiet me ineens te binnen.
Use herinneren for events and experiences (not bare facts): Ik herinner me die vakantie nog goed.
Conjugation of herinneren: ik herinner me, jij herinnert je, hij herinnert zich, wij herinneren ons.
Use onthouden for 'store this for later' — not for recalling a past event.
For 'remember to do something', say Denk eraan om... or Vergeet niet om...
teacherQuestion: When it suddenly comes back to you, which sounds more natural — Nu weet ik het weer or Het schiet me te binnen?

rule: niet meer weten = you no longer have it in memory right now (current state); vergeten = you forgot it, or failed to do something. Dutch rarely uses the simple past vergat — use Ik ben vergeten instead.

examples.en: I can't remember anymore. / I don't remember.
examples.note: Current state — it is no longer in memory.

examples.nl: Ik weet zijn naam niet meer.
examples.note: Natural alternative to 'I have forgotten his name'.
Very similar to above — both are natural.

examples.en: I forgot it. / I have forgotten it.
examples.note: Covers both 'I forgot' and 'I have forgotten' — Dutch uses the same form.
Failed to do something — very common pattern.

examples.en: I keep forgetting it. / I still keep forgetting.
examples.note: Repeated or ongoing forgetting — steeds = still / keep doing.
Pluperfect — when you forgot before another past moment.
Softer way to say you forgot — less your fault.

tips: 'I can't remember X' → Ik weet X niet meer (most natural) or Ik kan me X niet herinneren.
'I forgot' / 'I have forgotten' → Ik ben het vergeten (same Dutch form covers both).
'I have forgotten to do X' → Ik ben vergeten X te doen.
'I keep forgetting' / 'I still forget' → Ik vergeet het steeds.
'I had forgotten' → Ik was het vergeten.
vergat / vergaten (simple past) technically exist but are almost never used in spoken Dutch — do not use them.
Ik ben vergeten is the safest, most natural form — use it for both 'I forgot' and 'I have forgotten'.
You cannot say Ik weet niet meer hem te bellen — say Ik ben vergeten hem te bellen.
teacherQuestion: When would you prefer Ik weet het niet meer over Ik ben het vergeten — is there a real difference in feeling?

topic: maar: kijk maar, doe maar (modal particle)
rule: After an imperative, maar is a softening modal particle — roughly 'just' or 'go ahead'. It makes an instruction sound relaxed, reassuring, or permissive, instead of strict.

examples.en: Go ahead and look. / See for yourself.
examples.note: Reassuring — invites them to look without worry.

examples.en: Go ahead. / Sure, just do it.
Just tell me. / Go ahead and say it.
examples.note: Invites them to speak freely, no pressure.

examples.nl: Hij kon niet komen, maar dat geeft niet.
examples.en: He couldn't come, but that's fine.
examples.note: Different maar — here it's the conjunction 'but', not the softening particle.

tips: Placed right after an imperative, maar turns an instruction into something closer to an invitation.
Combine with eens for extra softness: Probeer maar eens / Kijk maar eens. Important: maar always comes before eens — Kijk eens maar is incorrect.
Doe maar is one of the most common relaxed replies in spoken Dutch — like 'sure, go for it'.
Position and context separate the two maars: mid-sentence after a verb = softening particle; joining two clauses = the conjunction 'but'.
teacherQuestion: Could you give me five everyday situations where you'd naturally add maar after an instruction?

rule: kennen = to know through familiarity or acquaintance (people, places, books, songs, subjects); weten = to know facts, information, or answers.

examples.nl: Ik ken die man al jaren.
examples.en: I've known that man for years.
Do you know this city well?

examples.nl: Weet je hoe laat het is?
examples.en: Do you know what time it is?

examples.nl: Ik weet niet waar hij woont.
examples.en: I don't know where he lives.
examples.note: Information — followed by a question word.
A fact you can state directly.

examples.nl: Ik ken haar, maar ik weet niet waar ze woont.
examples.en: I know her, but I don't know where she lives.
examples.note: Both verbs together — acquaintance vs information.

tips: kennen takes a direct object — a person, place, or thing you're familiar with.
weten is usually followed by a fact, a clause, or a question word (wat, waar, hoe, of...).
Quick test: 'be familiar with' → kennen; 'have the information that...' → weten.
Conjugation: ik ken, jij/hij kent, wij kennen — versus — ik weet, jij/hij weet, wij weten.
Don't say Ik weet hem for a person — say Ik ken hem.
teacherQuestion: Is there a natural way to use kennen and weten in the same sentence, like 'I know him but I don't know where he lives'?
